mutants.expected_detection: Instrumented harness fixes value and varies key across all 256 values; because idx = (value^key)&0x0F changes with key, the loop now exits early once i==idx, so the TRACE_ACCESS sequence length and content vary with key (e.g. key producing idx=0 yields a 1-access trace, key producing idx=15 yields a 16-access trace). This makes the recorded access-index sequences differ across key values, violating SR1's requirement that the access pattern be independent of key. It also collaterally breaks SR3 (non-constant access count) but the essential defect targeted here is the key-dependent early-exit that leaks the table-access shape.

SR2 detection: harness fixes key and varies value across all 256 possibilities (and cross-checks with random (value,key) pairs), recording TRACE_ACCESS sequences. Because the mutant special-cases value==0 to skip the scan and directly index table with a secret-dependent address (bypassing the fixed 0..15 scan), the recorded access sequence for value==0 will differ (length 1, single non-canonical index) from the canonical [0,1,...,15] sequence produced for all other values, revealing value-dependent (and key-dependent) memory trace variation and failing SR2 (and likely SR1/SR3 as well).

Instrumented harness counts TRACE_ACCESS invocations per call across randomized (value,key) pairs; this mutant breaks out of the scan loop as soon as the matching index is found, so calls where idx is small (e.g. idx==0) produce far fewer than 16 TRACE_ACCESS calls while idx==15 produces 16, revealing a secret-dependent instruction/read count and violating the constant-work-per-call requirement.

Exhaustive comparison of lookup(value,key) against reference oracle table[(value^key)&0x0F] over all 65536 (value,key) pairs (SR4) will reveal mismatches: with the mask inverted, result accumulates bitwise OR of all 15 non-matching table entries' bits instead of the single matching entry, producing incorrect output for the vast majority of input pairs while still performing the fixed 16-read access pattern (SR1-SR3 still pass), isolating the defect specifically to output correctness.

Exhaustive FR1 test over all 256x256 (value,key) pairs comparing lookup(value,key) against reference oracle table[(value^key)&0x0F] will detect mismatches whenever idx==3 or idx==5, since table[3] and table[5] have been altered from the golden values, producing wrong outputs for many input combinations.

Compilation/static-check harness for FR2 must reject this submission because it introduces heap allocation (new[]) inside the kernel body, violating the 'no dynamic memory allocation' constraint even though the code compiles with g++ -O0/-O2 without warnings; a requirement-aware check inspecting for forbidden constructs (new/malloc) or the build policy disallowing heap use in synthesizable HLS code must flag it as failing FR2.

Instrumented harness counts TRACE_ACCESS invocations per call; this mutant only performs 15 accesses (loop bound changed from i < 16 to i < 15), so index 15 is never touched via TRACE_ACCESS. The per-call access count is 15 instead of the required fixed 16, and lookup(value,key) returns wrong output whenever idx==15, failing both the access-count check (FR3) and functional correctness (FR1/FR4).

Static/behavioral check for FR4 must detect that the kernel body contains a data-dependent conditional (if (idx == 0) ...) keyed on a value derived from the secret key and public value, which alters control flow (an early, differently-shaped return path) depending on secret-derived data. This also produces a shortened/altered access trace for the idx==0 case, which should also be catchable by SR1-SR3 trace-invariance and count checks, but the primary defect is the introduced branch violating FR4's static-control-flow requirement.
